meta.title: Blog - Giovani HOUENOU
meta.description: Notes and insights on civil engineering, stage craft and public speaking.

title: Notes from site and stage
subtitle: Practical reflections on structure, presence and voice - for those who build, host and speak.

detail.ctaText: Let’s talk about your context - site, stage or speaking.

clarte-message-scene.title: A clear message before you take the stage
clarte-message-scene.excerpt: Before nerves and posture, there is one sentence. Here’s how to find it and hold it.
clarte-message-scene.lead: Many talks fail before the first mic. Not from a lack of charisma - from a lack of a single message.

sections.heading: One intention
paragraphs: Before working on voice or eye contact, ask: what should the audience remember in one sentence? If you can’t say it, they won’t either.
That sentence isn’t a marketing slogan. It’s the thread that guides every story, transition and silence.

sections.heading: Structure without rigidity
paragraphs: A simple structure is enough: context, stakes, proposal, call. The rest varies by format - pitch, panel or speech.
The common mistake: saying everything. Presence starts when you choose to cut.

sections.heading: Rehearse in real conditions
paragraphs: Rehearsing at a desk doesn’t prepare you for live. Time it, film it, change rooms. The body must learn the path of the message.

suivi-chantier-reporting.title: Site reporting: write to decide
suivi-chantier-reporting.excerpt: A useful report isn’t a novel. It helps the owner decide quickly.
suivi-chantier-reporting.lead: On a site, information is everywhere. What’s often missing is an actionable summary for those who carry decisions.

sections.heading: What the owner must see in 30 seconds
paragraphs: Progress, critical gaps, decisions requested. Everything else can live in an annex. Good reporting respects the reader’s time.
Annotated photos can beat an opaque technical paragraph.

sections.heading: Trace without drowning
paragraphs: Traceability protects the project. It shouldn’t turn every visit into an unreadable file. Choose milestones, not a flood of detail.

sections.heading: Escalate early
paragraphs: A gap flagged early costs less than a non-conformity found at the end of a phase. Reporting also builds that reflex.

rythme-antenne-live.title: Holding the pace live on air
rythme-antenne-live.excerpt: On air, time is an instrument. Here’s how to keep it without smothering the exchange.
rythme-antenne-live.lead: Live doesn’t forgive long hesitation. But it rewards real listening - the kind that moves an interview forward without rushing it.

sections.heading: The timing net
paragraphs: Before going live, know the segments, durations and escape hatches. Improvise, yes - without a net, no.
A prepared transition often saves an interview that drifts.

sections.heading: Listen to relaunch
paragraphs: The best follow-ups come from a detail you heard, not a sheet you read. Prepare angles, not rigid scripts.

sections.heading: Useful silence
paragraphs: A well-placed silence lets a guest go deeper. Too much silence empties the show. Dose makes the signature.

presence-corps-voix.title: Body and voice: one presence
presence-corps-voix.excerpt: Posture isn’t theatre. It’s the physical support of the message.
presence-corps-voix.lead: We separate content and delivery too often. Yet the body announces the talk before the first words.

sections.heading: Anchor before volume
paragraphs: Before projecting the voice, anchor your stance. A stable voice comes from a stable body - feet, hips, low breath.

sections.heading: Eye contact as connection
paragraphs: Scanning the room isn’t looking. Choose contact points, hold them for one idea, then move on.

sections.heading: Train the pair
paragraphs: Work voice and gesture together. Otherwise you’ll get fine diction on a body that contradicts the message.

coordination-moe-moa.title: When owner and design team don’t speak the same language
coordination-moe-moa.excerpt: The consulting engineer translates. Here’s how to avoid costly misunderstandings.
coordination-moe-moa.lead: On a project, tension often starts with fuzzy vocabulary. Clarifying roles and deliverables already secures the work.

sections.heading: Name the decisions
paragraphs: Who decides? On what criteria? With what deadline? Without answers, every meeting restarts the same debate.

sections.heading: Technical interface
paragraphs: Technical advisory is a bridge: rephrase the owner’s need into verifiable criteria for the design team, and escalate alerts without useless drama.

sections.heading: Document arbitrations
paragraphs: A forgotten oral call comes back as a non-conformity. A short dated shared note changes the project dynamic.

ceremonie-protocole.title: Protocol and flow: the MC paradox
ceremonie-protocole.excerpt: Honour protocol without freezing the room - the balance of a successful ceremony.
ceremonie-protocole.lead: An official ceremony demands precision. But precision without warmth becomes mechanical. The MC holds both.

sections.heading: The script as a score
paragraphs: A minute-by-minute run of show doesn’t kill improvisation: it frames it. You know where to return when something unexpected happens.

sections.heading: Coordinate backstage
paragraphs: Control room, protocol, speakers: the MC is the sync point. A clear brief before opening avoids awkward silences.

sections.heading: The right tone
paragraphs: Neither too solemn nor too casual. Tone follows the venue, the audience and the purpose of the evening - not the host’s ego.
